# Current state — legeos

What the project believes right now: live terms, constraints, policies and requirements, and what has been found or assessed. Decisions have their own view, `DECISION-HISTORY.md`.

## Terms

_(none)_

## Constraints

### The first release does not attempt a custom kernel, libc, package format/manager, display protocol, object filesystem, universal checkpointing, all NVIDIA generations, an app store, phone/tablet/server editions, or third-party shell extensions

`active` · `@legeos.constraint.first-release-scope/1` · scope `all` · topic `first-release-scope`

Until the five first-release claims are proven, LegeOS keeps systemd, cgroup v2, APT/Debian packages, standard filesystems, PipeWire, NetworkManager, BlueZ, Mesa and the upstream NVIDIA userspace stack. It does not build: a Linux kernel fork, a new package format or manager, a new libc/basic userland, replacement networking/Bluetooth/audio stacks, a new display protocol, a semantic/object filesystem replacing paths, transparent checkpointing of arbitrary applications, support for every old NVIDIA generation, a complete alternative application store, phone/tablet/server editions, or extensions/third-party shell plugins.

### Identity comes from the launch cgroup, never from a client's self-declared app_id; Exec= is never run through a shell; the governor is observe-only until traces are reviewed and never selects a victim by memory size alone

`active` · `@legeos.constraint.identity-and-launch-safety/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-appd/**"`, `path "crates/lege-window/**"`, `path "services/lege-resourced/**"` · topic `identity-launch-governor-safety`

(1) A window's application identity is resolved PID -> cgroup -> instance -> canonical AppId; client claims (Wayland app_id, WM_CLASS, sandbox id) can only lower confidence (claim mismatch) or, when unique, yield claim-only confidence — never override a verified launch, and privileged actions require verified-launch. (2) Applications are launched as the registered executable plus an argument vector in a dedicated systemd unit; Exec= lines are parsed, never passed to a shell. (3) lege-resourced ships observe-only; enforcement (memory.high, reclaim, checkpoint, cgroup.kill) is enabled in stages after recorded traces are reviewed; the victim score weighs growth, PSI contribution, foreground/visible state, unsaved work and disposability, never resident size alone; session-critical units are never candidates.

### Exactly one selected provider per exclusive system role may autostart

`active` · `@legeos.constraint.one-provider-per-role/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-session-core/src/autostart.rs"`, `path "crates/lege-session-core/src/providers.rs"`, `path "crates/lege-types/src/provider.rs"` · topic `one-provider-per-role`

For every ProviderRole (network-status-ui, notification-server, file-chooser, file-manager, lock-screen, association-broker, clipboard-manager, power-manager, screenshot-service, input-method, portal-backend, greeter) installing a second provider never silently starts both; the user or distribution policy selects one and only that one autostarts.

### Every component is a Debian package (nothing under /usr/local or untracked in $HOME); lege-window carries no async runtime or D-Bus dependency

`active` · `@legeos.constraint.packaging-and-render-thread/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-window/**"`, `path "debian/**"`, `path "tools/xtask/**"` · topic `packaging-and-render-thread`

All binaries, units, manifests and policy files are installed by Debian packages (cargo-deb now, the vendored source package later); development installs go through a local apt repository. The compositor-side lege-window crate must never depend on tokio, zbus, async-std or smol because it runs on the compositor render thread.

### System behaviour belongs in services; tray icons, panels and applets are views

`active` · `@legeos.constraint.services-not-indicators/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-session-core/**"`, `path "services/**"`, `path "shell/**"` · topic `services-not-indicators`

No policy (timezone discovery, power decisions, autostart choices, association defaults, notification storage) is implemented in a shell surface or applet; each lives in a service crate/daemon with a D-Bus interface, and the shell only renders and forwards user choices.

## Observations

### The live watcher never refreshed a directory's own metadata when its contents changed, so folders showed modification times from before their contents changed

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.a-directory-whose-contents-changed-kept-a-stale-modification-time/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/btrfs_delta.rs"`, `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/mutation.rs"`, `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/watch.rs"`

Three of the four Btrfs correctness-gate failures were bugs in shared index code that the delta merely exercised, and two of those were live on the inotify watcher's own path, where they had gone unnoticed because the watcher's tests compared namespaces and not metadata. (1) A write through one name of a hard link left the index's other names holding stale size and mtime; the watcher reaches this through IN_MODIFY on a linked file. Fixed by mirroring a write to an inode's other names, gated on nlink > 1 so the common case costs one probe on entries_object. (2) A move onto an already-occupied path aborted the batch with UNIQUE constraint failed: entries.root_id, entries.path_bytes; the watcher reaches this through rename(2) over an existing destination, which is what every editor's atomic save does. Fixed by having the move take the occupant's row over. (3) The largest one: a directory whose entries changed never had its own metadata re-read, so its mtime and ctime in the index were from before its contents changed — a folder in a file manager showing a modification time older than the files it contains. inotify names the child; nothing tells the index the parent's own mtime moved. Found by upgrading tests/watch.rs to the same field-for-field metadata comparison the delta harness uses, which failed immediately with exactly one differing row in each nested-rename test: the directory the rename happened in. Fixed by having WatchOwner::pump re-read a directory that gained or lost an entry, one extra lstat per pump, so unpacking 10,000 files into a directory costs one stat rather than 10,000. The same metadata upgrade also caught a retarget_subtree path with a trailing separator from Path::join(""), equal to its sibling for every Path comparison but a different byte string as an index key; six hand-written test streams describing sequences no kernel emits, which had been passing by agreeing with each other rather than with the filesystem; and one unit test that asserted the mtime bug outright. There is now a single metadata-comparison definition (crates/lege-file-index/tests/support/entry_facts.rs) shared by the Btrfs harness, the delta unit tests and the watcher tests, so the asymmetry that hid all of this cannot reopen. The general lesson is that a namespace-only comparison cannot see a whole class of index defect, and the delta lane's value was not confined to the backend it was measuring.

### Unreadable and unwatchable directories do not make a scan incomplete, so the index claims Current over subtrees it never saw

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.a-pass-that-could-not-read-every-directory-still-commits-current/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/generation.rs"`, `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/reconcile.rs"`

ScanSession::commit (crates/lege-file-index/src/generation.rs:291-293) derives completeness as `limited.is_none() && permission_denied == 0 && !cancel.is_cancelled()`. The `unreadable_dirs` counter is incremented by ScanSession::note_unreadable (generation.rs:187) and reported in the outcome (generation.rs:315), but is never consulted by that test. Reconcile's Walk::note_unreadable (reconcile.rs:167-173) sets its own ReconcileReport.complete = false and then calls session.note_unreadable(denied) with denied = false for a directory that could not be armed or read for any non-permission reason. The result is that the ReconcileReport knows the pass was partial while the committed generation does not: the root commits as RootState::Current, and collect_tombstones — which runs only when complete — treats every row it failed to observe as deleted. On the reference laptop this is not hypothetical, because 189,089 home directories against a 125,037 watch budget means arm_recursive refuses watches and stops descending on every single pass. This breaks the invariant the crate states for itself, that nothing enters Current but a complete pass, and acceptance gate 3 of docs/planning/shared-incremental-file-index.md, that overflow, offline and partial states cannot be mistaken for current complete data. The watcher lane added a compensating check in WatchLoop::repair that compares watches_refused across a pass and re-marks the root stale, but the defect is in the core: unreadable_dirs must be folded into commit()'s completeness test, which also changes tombstone collection for every caller.

### The delta decoder joined subvolume-relative paths onto the index root, so almost every change was dropped as vanished

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.a-send-stream-names-paths-relative-to-the-subvolume-not-the-index-root/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/btrfs_delta.rs"`

The Btrfs delta correctness gate was run for the first time against a real loopback fixture on 2026-09-04 and failed. btrfs send emits every path relative to the root of the snapshotted subvolume, but btrfs_delta::to_mutations resolved each one with target.root_path.join(relative) (btrfs_delta.rs:924) and FsMetadata lstat'd it under the same index root (btrfs_delta.rs:760). The fixture snapshots @home while indexing @home/bench, so a created file arrived as bench/inbox/new000.txt and was resolved to @home/bench/bench/inbox/new000.txt, which does not exist; the path was then counted as vanished and silently dropped. a_delta_equals_a_fresh_scan failed at the first non-empty scenario with 102 differences, every new path missing from the delta index and the parent directory differing only in mtime because nothing had been applied; the edge-case test failed with 933 differences and a report of 9 planned paths, 1 mutation and 8 vanished. The no-change scenario passed, because an empty delta is the correct answer there, which is why the defect looked like a working backend in unit tests. The existing unit tests could not catch it: they set root_path to /home/dk and supply stream paths implicitly relative to that same directory, assuming the subvolume root and the index root are the same path. That assumption is false in production as well as in the fixture, because @home is the subvolume and mounts at /home, so the index root is /home/<user>, a strict subdirectory; a delta of @home also names other users' paths, which must be skipped rather than applied to this user's root. Two distinct counters are needed, because conflating a path outside the index root with a path that vanished from disk is what hid the bug.

### A Trash1 smoke test run against the real session bus emptied the user's actual volume trash

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.agent-smoke-test-emptied-a-real-volume-trash/1` · scope `path "cli/lege/**"`, `path "services/lege-filed/**"`

While smoke-testing `lege trash empty --yes` end to end, the implementing agent constructed TrashApi with TrashMounts::System instead of TrashMounts::Fixed, so the sweep read the machine's real mount table, found /media/dk/4668959A68958977/.Trash-1000, and permanently deleted its one entry — a folder named `target` (a Rust build directory, regenerable) trashed on 2026-08-30. Unrecoverable. The code behaved as designed; the harness choice was the fault: TrashMounts::Fixed exists precisely so tests cannot reach real disks, every committed test uses it, and the offending smoke script was removed rather than left as a trap. Standing rule going forward: any end-to-end exercise of destructive file operations must run against fixture mounts (TrashMounts::Fixed, a throwaway HOME and XDG_DATA_HOME) — never the developer host's real mount table.

### A user can take the read-only checkpoints but cannot send the delta between them, so the delta backend is split across the privilege boundary

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.btrfs-send-needs-privilege-but-snapshotting-does-not/1` · scope `path "services/lege-hostd/src/index_checkpoint.rs"`

Probed on a loopback Btrfs fixture with the declared LegeOS subvolume layout (@, @home, @var, @snapshots, @deployments), kernel 6.17, btrfs-progs 6.16, by running scripts/btrfs-index-fixture.sh probe as root and comparing against the same operations run as uid 1000. As the unprivileged owner of the subvolume: btrfs subvolume snapshot -r succeeds, and a second read-only snapshot succeeds. btrfs send --no-data -p fails, and btrfs subvolume delete fails, the latter despite the filesystem being mounted with user_subvol_rm_allowed. Run as root the same send produced 450 bytes of metadata delta, confirming the operation itself is sound and only the privilege is missing. The consequence for the architecture is that the delta backend cannot live wholly in the per-user lege-filed: taking a checkpoint could, but producing the delta between two of them requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN and must go through lege-hostd, as must discarding a spent checkpoint. That in turn forces the transport question, because the stream lege-hostd writes is mode 0600 and root-owned while the daemon that must read it runs as the user, and a metadata delta names every path under @home so it must not be made world-readable.

### btrfs send --no-data is flat in tree size and proportional to the change, and the delta beats a crawl by up to 647x

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.delta-catch-up-cost-tracks-the-change-and-beats-a-crawl-except-on-bulk-creation/4` · scope `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/btrfs_delta.rs"`

The final measurement, run as root against a loopback Btrfs fixture on 2026-09-04 at commit 8d74542, across three tree sizes and eight scenarios, with the correctness gate passing for the first time. The architectural question this lane existed to answer was whether btrfs send itself is proportional to the change rather than to the tree, because a send proportional to the tree reduces the whole idea to a cheaper crawl. It is flat. The same change sent between snapshots of trees two orders of magnitude apart costs: nothing at all, 1.6 / 1.7 / 1.9 ms with a byte-identical 113 B stream; a whole-directory rename (4 paths), 2.4 / 2.4 / 2.8 ms, 481 B; an hour of desktop use (67 paths), 4.1 / 5.5 / 5.9 ms, 13.6 KiB; 100 new files (102 paths), 3.7 / 5.8 / 7.0 ms, 34.0 KiB; a build burst (7,007 paths), 128.7 / 148.7 / 149.3 ms, 2.7 MiB; one 1 GiB file (2 paths), 20.7 / 29.2 / 20.3 ms, 408.4 KiB. Stream size is identical across tree sizes in every row; residual send drift across a hundredfold tree is under 4 ms. Send is proportional to the change instead: at 153,327 entries, 1.9 ms at 0 changed paths, 2.8 at 4, 5.9 at 67, 7.0 at 102, 149.3 at 7,007 and 1,185.4 at 50,003 — roughly 24 microseconds per changed path above a 2 ms floor. End to end at 153,327 entries: an hour of desktop use 30.4 ms against 19,657.6 (647x), 100 new files 37.8 against 19,198.3 (508x), a whole-directory rename 49.4 against 19,577.1 (396x), truncate-chmod-rewrite 46.8 against 16,865.9 (361x), one 1 GiB file 39.1 against 11,329.3 (290x), nothing at all 71.1 against 17,588.2 (248x), a build burst 1,269.1 against 18,636.6 (15x), a mass delete of 50,003 rows 6,095.2 against 14,202.7 (2.3x). The two weak rows are the architecture working, not failing: the build burst is slower than a crawl only on the 1,540-entry tree (0.4x) and barely ahead at 15,339 (1.3x), a crossover of a few thousand entries that no real home reaches, and 2,001 of its paths were excluded by coverage policy before reaching the index; the mass delete's 2.3x is 4,910 of its 6,095 ms spent writing 50,003 tombstones, which the crawl arm pays too. --no-data holds for large files but scales with extents rather than bytes: a 1 GiB file yields 408.4 KiB in 8,200 commands, about one UPDATE_EXTENT per 128 KiB extent, so a dormant window writing 100 GiB costs on the order of 40 MiB of stream and there should be a cap above which the backend gives up and asks for a reconcile. The delta arm reads 0 block-layer bytes in all 24 rows against the crawl's 116-159 MiB, with the caveat that read_bytes is /proc/self/io of the harness process and btrfs send is a child, so the send's own reads are unmeasured; its 5.9 ms wall time bounds them to a few MiB. The full table is docs/measurements/btrfs-delta-measured.md, written by the harness. This supersedes revision 3, whose figures came from the third of five runs, before the last two correctness bugs were fixed.

### fanotify refuses a filesystem mark on a Btrfs subvolume, and one group cannot hold marks on two subvolumes at all — so it cannot cover LegeOS's declared layout

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.fanotify-cannot-span-btrfs-subvolumes/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-fanotify/**"`, `path "distro/deploy/layout.toml"`

fanotify_test_fsid in fs/notify/fanotify/fanotify_user.c (Linux v6.17) returns -EXDEV for a dentry whose statfs fsid differs from its superblock root's — the kernel comment names Btrfs subvolumes explicitly — and grants the weak-fsid fallback only when mark_type == FAN_MARK_INODE. FAN_MARK_FILESYSTEM and FAN_MARK_MOUNT therefore cannot mark @home, and distro/deploy/layout.toml:44 declares @, @home, @var, @snapshots and @deployments, all subvolumes. Independently, fanotify_set_mark_fsid refuses to hold weak-fsid marks from two different Btrfs subvolumes in one group, and one EventSource is one group — so even the unprivileged inode-mark variant could not watch @home and @ together, which inotify has no trouble with. The same weak-fsid guard was reproduced on this ext4/tmpfs/fuse host, where the fuse project drive reports fsid [0,0] (also weak): marking it in a group that already holds a tmpfs or ext4 mark returns EXDEV, and so does the reverse order, while two strong fsids (tmpfs then ext4) mix freely. Consequence for this machine: the 172,681-directory fuse project drive can be watched by a fanotify group only if that group watches nothing else. The FAN_MARK_FILESYSTEM path itself needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN and is not directly measured here; scripts/fanotify-privileged-probe.sh collects that one privileged step for the user to run against Lane E's Btrfs loopback fixture.

### Third hands-on run at the installed desktop: Files object inert by pointer, band over client content, no window controls, no resize route

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.hands-on-run-3-findings-20260903/1` · scope `path "apps/lege-files/**"`, `path "compositor/lege-comp/**"`, `path "crates/lege-window/**"`, `path "shell/lege-shell/**"`

User logged into the LegeOS desktop at cb57689 (installed packages match HEAD) to test in-place hot-fixing and reports: (1) redundant HOME labels on the left of the file manager; (2) Copy path does nothing and no button in the file manager works; (3) a bare Super press hides windows but not the open file manager; (4) windows have no minimize or close buttons; (5) Kitty's top line is cut off by the window pane; (6) windows move but do not resize. Usability otherwise possible but poor. Diagnosis from the code: the 'file manager' is the shell's expanded Files object on Home (Layer::HomeSurface), so a reveal never hides it and its rail read Home ▸ Home over PLACE Home; single click activated rows, so the selection-gated file verbs stayed inert; spawn_copy_path rendered the text and never put it on a clipboard; the compositor painted its 32 px recovery band OVER the client's top strip (hiding client-side close buttons and a terminal's first line) and offered only a 24 px corner grip for resizing.

### Hands-on run 4 (2026-09-03): the deploy stopped at hostd, snap browsers cannot connect, bands render above every window, no screen timeout, the launcher could not find snap applications

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.hands-on-run-4-findings-20260903/1` · scope `path "cli/lege/src/dev/**"`, `path "compositor/lege-comp/**"`, `path "services/lege-hostd/**"`, `path "services/lege-sessiond/src/background/desktop_import.rs"`, `path "shell/lege-shell/src/omnibox.rs"`

Also reported: no right-click menu in the Files object; windows fight for focus; text input is snappier than COSMIC.

### Fifth hands-on run: the file manager is one full-screen mode, previews bleed through translucent windows, Home is mostly empty and labels repeat what icons should say

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.hands-on-run-5-findings-20260904/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-field/**"`, `path "shell/lege-shell/**"`

The user, working inside the installed LegeOS desktop, reported six things. (1) The Files object takes the whole screen and only one can be open, so there is no way to hold two directories at once. (2) Window previews on the Home Field show through translucent clients — a kitty with background_opacity under 1 shows the field, and the field's own live preview of that kitty, through itself. On reflection the user's rule is stronger than suppressing previews: nothing of Home should be visible through a translucent window at all, only the windows behind it. (3) Home is mostly empty space, against the rule that there is to be no useless space; the largest object on it, a folder tile, drew its path in dim text and nothing else. (4) The XDG Desktop folder should be a small expandable tray on Home rather than absent or large. (5) The Files rail repeats itself: 'Documents / Standard folder' says the same thing twice where every other desktop uses an icon, and standard Ubuntu theme icons are what it should use. (6) The drag grid is too coarse to aim with. Separately, the user wants a route to a bootable LegeOS they can develop from, with WiFi through NetworkManager and nm-tray-2, so that Lubuntu can be deleted.

### Why the Home Field failed at a real desktop: four typing defects, an inverted rung rule, an unregistered interface and a mixed-age install

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.home-hands-on-failures-diagnosed/1` · scope `path "apps/lege-greeter/**"`, `path "compositor/lege-comp/**"`, `path "services/lege-sessiond/**"`, `path "shell/lege-shell/**"`

A desktop tester reported that typing was slow and error-prone, that there was no logout control, and that the shutdown control was always visible and did nothing. Every cause was located and none was a regression; all were present in a workspace-green tree.

Typing, four independent defects. (1) Both winit surfaces translated a key press with `.chars().next()`, but `Key::Character` carries a `SmolStr` because a dead-key or compose commit with no precomposed form arrives as base letter plus combining mark in one event — the remainder was dropped silently (shell/lege-shell/src/surface/window.rs:125 and the identical copy in apps/lege-greeter/src/surface/window.rs, where the field is a password). (2) The compositor asked for `XkbConfig::default()` — empty rules/model/layout/variant and `options: None` — so no configured layout was honoured and no Compose key existed (compositor/lege-comp/src/state.rs:205). (3) `ensure_launcher_icons` ran on the winit event-loop thread on every redraw, and every accepted key requests a redraw: each miss read .desktop files across every XDG_DATA_DIRS entry, stat-ed a candidate per size bucket per extension per theme directory, then decoded a PNG or rasterized an SVG at 128x128, between a key press and the frame showing its character (shell/lege-shell/src/surface/app.rs:501, shell/lege-shell/src/icons.rs:241-367). (4) Full repaint and full-buffer present per keystroke with no damage tracking, which sets the latency floor the third defect then exceeds. `pixelkit_shell::Input` holds `keys` as a Vec, so no key is dropped by queueing.

Power controls. The session widget declared `session.lock` and `session.poweroff` at `Representation::Small` and `session.logout` at `Wide` (shell/lege-shell/src/surface/widgets/mod.rs:102-108), while a system tile is created at its floor span and stays there (shell/lege-shell/src/field_model.rs:227) — so on every real desktop the destructive action was the one that could not be hidden and the safe one was behind a resize the default density makes inert. Separately, `Session.Lifecycle1` was registered only if the system-bus connection had succeeded at sessiond startup, with no retry, unlike `Location1` two lines above (services/lege-sessiond/src/main.rs:388-409, 552-564): losing that race removed every power control for the whole session. Every failure path in the shell's `spawn_lifecycle` was a `tracing::error!` and nothing on screen, and `draw_region_strip` never consulted logind's Can* verdicts, so a control known to be refused was drawn identically to a working one.

Install coherence. The installed set was mixed-age: ten of thirteen LegeOS packages were more than a day older than lege-shell, so a 2026-08-25 shell was calling interfaces and protocol requests that the 2026-08-22 sessiond and 2026-08-23 compositor predate.

### Home's three-second refresh profiled: what was fixed, and the two service-side costs that remain

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.home-refresh-costs-profiled-20260902/1` · scope `path "services/lege-sessiond/src/apis/audio.rs"`, `path "services/lege-sessiond/src/apis/lifecycle.rs"`, `path "shell/lege-shell/**"`

Measured against a live sessiond on the development host, one pass of the Home Surface's three-second refresh loop cost about 82ms, of which: fetch_apps 34ms, fetch_settings_widget 19ms, fetch_session_widget 18ms, fetch_all(20) 5.5ms, fetch_projects 2.6ms, fetch_browser_sources 0.8ms. Separately, zbus's Connection::session() builds a new connection — socket, SASL handshake, Hello and a reader task — on every call, and the shell called it from three dozen places; caching one connection per tokio runtime took fetch_all from 14ms to 5.5ms.

Fixed in 392bd0d and f148046: the connection cache, joining the loop's independent fetches, joining the Session widget's three logind Can* questions (18ms to 13ms), and moving the application-catalogue read onto AppIdentity1.ApplicationsChanged plus a thirty-second backstop. An ordinary tick is now about 27ms.

Two costs remain and both are inside lege-sessiond, not the shell. Audio1.Get spawns `wpctl` as a child process on every call, which is most of fetch_settings_widget's remaining time; the Home Settings widget therefore spawns a process every three seconds for as long as the session lasts. Lifecycle1's Can* answers still cost about 13ms even when the three are asked together, which suggests the system-bus round trips to logind are being serialised inside sessiond rather than by the caller; logind's answer to whether this machine may shut down does not change between two three-second ticks and is a candidate for caching.

### The home tree needs half again more inotify watches than the index's budget allows, so watcher exhaustion is the normal outcome rather than an edge case

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.home-tree-exceeds-the-inotify-watch-budget/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/watch.rs"`

Measured on the reference laptop (kernel 6.17) on 2026-09-04: $HOME holds 230,323 directories, and 189,089 after applying the index's own skip list (189,087 with a depth<=24 clamp, so depth is not a factor). The project drive /mnt/Samsung980_1TB adds a further 172,681 directories. fs.inotify.max_user_watches is 250,074 and WatchBudget::from_limits deliberately takes half of it, giving 125,037. A single home root therefore requires about 1.5x the budget the index allows itself, and a full drive index would require about 1.6x the entire per-user kernel allowance. The consequence is that arm_recursive refuses watches past the budget, marks the pass incomplete and stops descending, so the root commits as Stale{WatcherExhausted} on every reconcile: the WatcherExhausted fallback path is the steady state on this machine, not an exceptional condition. This also contradicts the figure of 157,283 post-skip directories recorded in crates/lege-file-index/src/watch.rs and .agent/scratch/de01/F2-plan.md on 2026-09-03; the discrepancy is not explained by depth clamping and is left for the benchmark lane to settle from the index's own policy. Both figures exceed the budget, so the conclusion holds either way.

### Index baseline measurements (2026-09-04): watch-budget shortfall confirmed, idle-wakeup fix confirmed at 0

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.index-baseline-2026-09-04/1`

Measured on the reference laptop (kernel 6.17, ext4) via `cargo run -q -p xtask -- index-bench`: $HOME holds 189,094 post-skip directories (RootPolicy::default_home), 1.51x WatchBudget::max_watches (125,037) and 0.76x the whole-kernel fs.inotify.max_user_watches allowance (250,074) — confirming a home root cannot stay fully watched under inotify on this machine by construction. ### Index1's GenerationAdvanced and RootStateChanged signals are implemented but never wired, so no client can observe the index changing

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.index-change-signals-never-fire/1` · scope `path "services/lege-filed/src/index_host.rs"`, `path "services/lege-filed/src/main.rs"`

Index1Signals in services/lege-filed/src/index_host.rs implements index_core::ChangeSink and can emit both GenerationAdvanced and RootStateChanged, but nothing calls Index::set_change_sink (crates/lege-file-index/src/lib.rs) in this build; its own doc comment records the gap. Both signals are therefore dead: a client watching the index for changes receives nothing, and every consumer must poll. This blocks the adaptive-observer design, whose CatchingUp/Resuming step depends on telling an arriving consumer that a fresher generation has committed. A second defect is latent in the same type: Index1Signals calls bare tokio::spawn, but ChangeSink is a synchronous trait invoked from the plain std::thread watcher loop (services/lege-filed/src/watcher.rs), and tokio::spawn panics when called outside a runtime context. Wiring the sink without also capturing a tokio::runtime::Handle would therefore panic on the first mutation, unwind the watcher thread, and leave the daemon running but permanently blind — a worse failure than the dead signal it replaces.

**derived_from** `@legeos.work.file-index-maintenance/1`

### There is no OpenURI backend interface to implement: the portal frontend owns OpenURI, and launches the handler outside LegeOS identity

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.openuri-is-the-frontends-portal/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-associationd/**"`, `path "portals/xdg-desktop-portal-lege/**"`

`org.freedesktop.impl.portal.OpenURI` does not exist. On the declared Ubuntu base, `xdg-desktop-portal 1.20.3+ds-1ubuntu1.1` knows 25 impl interfaces and OpenURI is not among them (`strings /usr/libexec/xdg-desktop-portal | grep 'impl.portal'`); no `/usr/share/dbus-1/interfaces/*OpenURI*` XML is installed; and none of the six installed backends (gtk, kde, cosmic, lxqt, kwallet, gnome-keyring) claims it. The frontend implements `org.freedesktop.portal.OpenURI` itself: it finds the default handler through GAppInfo and `mimeapps.list`, delegates only the 'which application' question to `org.freedesktop.impl.portal.AppChooser`, and then launches the chosen desktop entry in its own scope.

Two consequences for LegeOS, both live at this commit. First, the launch does not go through `Launcher1`, so a file opened from a browser is not started into a LegeOS cgroup; since identity comes from the cgroup by design, that process is anonymous to `AppIdentity1` and to every policy keyed on it. Second, `lege-associationd` regenerates its `mimeapps.list` export after every association mutation (`crates/lege-associationd/src/dbus.rs`) but nothing writes it at session start (`services/lege-sessiond/src/main.rs` wires `AssociationApi` without an initial export), so a fresh home — or one whose file was removed — can disagree with `Associations1` until something changes a default.

The portal backend was corrected to match this reality rather than to claim an OpenURI interface nothing would call: `legeos.portal` still claims exactly four interfaces, and the AppChooser leg was fixed to recognise a LegeOS canonical app id among the desktop file ids the frontend offers (`AppIdentity1.ListApplications`), which is what makes the LegeOS default actually win.

### A reconcile that finds nothing changed costs as much as one that finds a hundred changes, and both scale with the tree

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.reconciliation-cost-tracks-tree-size-not-change-size/2` · scope `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/mutation.rs"`, `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/reconcile.rs"`

Re-measured on a quiet machine at 2026-09-04 13:25, after every lane had stopped compiling. Recursive reconciliation with the change set held fixed and the tree grown, release build, warm page cache (read_bytes zero throughout, so these are best-case): 1,000 files / 1,540 entries took 16 ms to acquire, 21 ms to reconcile with nothing changed and 26 ms with 100 files changed; 10,000 files / 15,339 entries took 157 / 281 / 254 ms; 100,000 files / 153,327 entries took 1,867 ms to acquire, 3,240 ms with nothing changed and 3,375 ms with 100 files changed. The architectural conclusion is unchanged and is the point of the record: reconcile cost is proportional to tree size and essentially blind to how much actually changed, so it cannot serve as steady-state maintenance. By contrast Index::apply is now flat in tree size after the accelerator-index work: a warm single-mutation batch costs 0.2 ms at 15,339 entries and 0.3 ms at 153,327, against 2.7 ms and 41.9 ms before, and a 100-mutation batch at 153,327 entries costs 4.1 ms against 43.1 ms before. A crawl therefore costs roughly 790x a hundred-mutation batch at this size. This revision corrects revision 1, which recorded 32,838 ms acquisition and 39,594 ms no-change reconcile at 153,326 entries: those figures were about ten times too high because they were taken while four other lanes were compiling on the same machine. Removing the new accelerator index leaves the reconcile at 2,027 / 3,420 ms, confirming the correction is a quieter machine rather than the index work. Any figure in docs/measurements/btrfs-delta-2026-09-04.md derived from the original run is wrong by roughly an order of magnitude and should be read against this record.

**supersedes** `@legeos.observation.reconciliation-cost-tracks-tree-size-not-change-size/1` · **derived_from** `@legeos.work.adaptive-index-maintenance/1`

### The reference laptop has one 55.9 GiB free tail, a 100 MiB ESP, and a provisioner that only takes a whole disk

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.this-machines-partition-table-cannot-hold-legeos-as-it-stands/1` · scope `path "distro/**"`, `path "installer/**"`

Measured on the reference laptop. nvme0n1 (953.9 GiB) holds NTFS 536G, NTFS 949M, Lubuntu's ext4 root 416G with 8.7G free, the 100 MiB ESP and a 16 MiB partition, leaving a 0.5 GiB free tail. nvme1n1 (931.5 GiB) holds a 16 MiB partition and the 875.6 GiB NTFS projects partition, leaving 55.9 GiB unallocated at its tail. Three consequences. (1) The only place a LegeOS root can go without destroying Lubuntu or Windows is that 55.9 GiB tail, which fits a 1 GiB ESP and a ~54 GiB btrfs root but not a 42 GiB target directory. (2) distro/deploy/layout.toml requires an ESP of 512M-1G and the existing one is 100 MiB, sandwiched between Lubuntu's root and a 16 MiB partition, so a second ESP on nvme1n1 is the answer rather than growing it. (3) installer/provision.sh runs sgdisk --zap-all on its target and has no mode that consumes free space beside existing partitions, so it cannot be run on this machine at all as it stands. Separately: five Cargo path dependencies point outside the repository, so a LegeOS installation could not rebuild LegeOS; mmdebstrap and debootstrap are not installed on this host; and nm-tray-2 is neither packaged nor named in the seed declaration.

### Omarchy launches applications into transient systemd units too, then identifies windows by self-declared app_id anyway

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.transient-unit-launch-converged-independently/2` · scope `path "crates/lege-appd/**"`, `path "crates/lege-types/**"`

Basecamp's Omarchy independently arrived at the same launch primitive LegeOS uses: bin/omarchy-launch-browser and five sibling scripts start applications with `systemd-run --user --collect --unit="omarchy-browser-$(date +%s%N)"`, giving one transient unit and therefore one cgroup per launch. It then does not use it. There is no reference to a cgroup, a unit or /proc/<pid>/cgroup anywhere under shell/; the shell identifies windows purely from the client's self-declared app_id (12 references). The cgroup exists and the information is discarded. This sharpens what LegeOS's identity model actually contributes: not that a per-launch cgroup exists, but that naming it app-legeos-<AppId>@<InstanceId>.service makes the cgroup name carry the identity, so a window's PID resolves to a cgroup, the cgroup name resolves to an AppId, and the governor, the dock and the notification router all key off one fact nobody had to ask the client for. Omarchy's unit name is a timestamp and carries no identity, so it cannot make that journey even though it has the cgroup. Independent convergence on the primitive is evidence the primitive is right; the naming convention is the part that turns it into an identity system, and is the part to defend in review.

**supersedes** `@legeos.observation.transient-unit-launch-converged-independently/1`

### Undoing a trash restored nothing and still committed — and the covering test hid it by substituting its own inputs

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.trash-undo-reported-a-restore-it-did-not-perform/1` · scope `path "services/lege-filed/**"`

Undo of a trash operation reported success and moved no file. undo_of built the undo plan from the operation's own paths — the pre-trash locations, the only ones OperationKind::Trash retains — so plan emitted Step::RestoreFromTrash aimed at a path the file had just vacated; execute found nothing there, took that for 'already restored', returned Ok, and the operation reached Committed. Ctrl+Z in the Files app and lege files undo both told the user the file was back when it was still in the trash. The same defect existed in the other direction, undoing a restore, with no test coverage at all.

What matters beyond the fix: the test that should have caught this concealed it. trashing_and_undoing_it_round_trip took undo_of's result, discarded its paths, looked the real trashed paths up itself via trash::list, and passed those in — a substitution production never performs. The test therefore exercised a path no caller takes and passed for four months while the production path was broken. A test that repairs its subject's output before asserting on it is not covering that subject; the repair is the bug, made invisible.

Fixed at git:464e069b7b2769bc5e0ab34e8191b65f9101e7db by recording where the trash actually put each item into the executed step, the way Move's undo already reads its RenameInPlace destination. A post-hoc trash::list lookup could not serve: trash::free_name resolves collisions against the live directory, so a path trashed twice leaves two records and nothing outside the operation can say which is which. The corrected test feeds undo_of straight into plan; reverting the fix fails it.

### Unprivileged fanotify is one mark per directory, arms 2.5x slower than inotify and costs about twice the memory, for 6.4% more headroom

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.unprivileged-fanotify-costs-more-per-directory-than-inotify/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-fanotify/**"`, `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/watch.rs"`

Measured on the reference laptop (kernel 6.17, ext4, uid 1000, no capabilities) over 100,000 directories, three runs, spread under 3%: inotify arms at 0.8-0.9 us per directory, fanotify inode marks at 2.1-2.2 us. Kernel SUnreclaim per directory is 104-106 B for inotify and 78-81 B for fanotify; process VmRSS per directory is 68 B for inotify and 287 B for fanotify, because every fanotify event in fid mode names its directory by opaque file handle and open_by_handle_at(2) is EPERM without CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH, so the handle-to-path map must live in userspace at one entry per directory. Totals: ~172 B per directory for inotify against ~366 B for fanotify. Against the kernel ceiling, 189,089 directories are 75.6% of fs.inotify.max_user_watches (250,074) and 71.1% of fs.fanotify.max_user_marks (266,105) — 6.4% more headroom where a home root needs 51% more than the index's WatchBudget. On throughput the two are indistinguishable: identical raw event counts and kinds for a create+write workload (40,000 events from 40,000 operations) and for a cargo-build-shaped create+write+rename+delete burst (100,000 events from 80,000 operations), within 2% on delivery rate, and both overflow at exactly 16,385 events with nothing reading the fd. Unprivileged fanotify also requires a fid-reporting mode: FAN_CLASS_NOTIF with no fid flags, FAN_UNLIMITED_QUEUE, FAN_MARK_MOUNT and FAN_MARK_FILESYSTEM are all EPERM.

## Assessments

### Desktop test-readiness audit — strong logic tests, missing system validation and core interaction surfaces

`verified` · `@legeos.assessment.desktop-test-readiness-20260827/1` · scope `path "apps/**"`, `path "ci/**"`, `path "compositor/**"`, `path "portals/**"`, `path "scripts/**"`, `path "services/**"`, `path "shell/**"`, `path "tests/**"`

LegeOS has a large, currently green unit/property test base, but the desktop cannot yet be considered system-tested: the integration harness does not start or drive a real composed session, the documented hardware runner is inert, installation/greeter/recovery/hardware paths remain manual, and several ordinary desktop interactions still have no graphical implementation.

- `#accessibility-and-localisation` — The repository ships accessibility and localisation intentions, but no AT-SPI/accessibility-tree implementation or runtime Fluent loader is present in the audited sources.
- `#automated-foundation` — All 1,015 workspace tests, lint/format checks, runtime smoke, and seven structural/action gates pass on the audited working tree.
- `#desktop-capability-gaps` — Graphical Settings is still a text renderer; FileChooser, AppChooser and Background portal prompts use NoUiAvailable; session lock is NotSupported; notifications are stored but not rendered; and power profiles are stored without idle/lid/brightness/battery actuation.
- `#false-green-risks` — The smoke test imports developer-host application state and tolerates an UNHEALTHY boot-health report, Home's offscreen test checks PNG validity and dimensions rather than rendered pixels, CI builds only the sessiond Debian package, and compositor-active boot health is explicitly unwired.
- `#hardware-runner-noop` — `lege doctor --hardware` produces byte-identical output to ordinary doctor because Context.hardware is never consumed; tests/hardware/*.toml is currently passive checklist data.
- `#system-test-gap` — There is no automated greetd-to-Home login, nested compositor input/render interaction, installed multi-package session, VM first-boot, shell-death recovery, or real-hardware execution path.

### Home Field usability audit — a deliberate divergence is a gap only where its substitute is missing, weaker or undiscoverable

`verified` · `@legeos.assessment.home-field-usability-gaps-20260831/1` · scope `path "apps/**"`, `path "compositor/**"`, `path "portals/**"`, `path "services/lege-filed/**"`, `path "shell/**"`

Audited the Home Field and the modules around it against mainstream desktop expectations. The Home Field's rejections — no taskbar, no tray, no virtual desktops, no title bars — are the product, so this audit judges each one by its substitute rather than by the convention it dropped, and reports a gap only where the substitute is missing, weaker or undiscoverable. On that test the shell's own rejections mostly hold; what fails is a different class of thing entirely — capabilities the project intends to have, believes it has, or documents as shipped, which are absent in code.

JUDGED BY SUBSTITUTE, AND SOUND. Virtual desktops: rejected by the one-workspace invariant (compositor/COMPOSITOR.md:12); substitute is park-to-tile plus show-all plus Alt-Tab; the substitute is real, but window.park has no chord at all and window.show-all has no pointer route outside one context menu, so the gap is discoverability, not the missing workspaces. Taskbar: rejected; substitute is the field's own app and parked-session tiles, which is a genuine replacement. Tray: rejected under the services-not-indicators constraint; substitute is the widget system plus ProviderRole slots, which works for network via the user's nm-tray2 but leaves a third-party app no place to dock. Title bars: no server-side chrome renderer, so decoration is forced client-side (compositor/lege-comp/src/xdg_shell.rs:467); the substitute for close is a context-menu row and for resize a compositor-painted grip, but there is no user-facing maximize control at all — a window only maximizes if the app asks.

GENUINE GAPS, RANKED BY DAILY COST. (1) No multi-select anywhere: the field carries a single focus: Option<TileId> (shell/lege-shell/src/surface/field_screen.rs:157) and the drawer browser a single entry_focus: usize (surface/file_browser.rs:54); no shift-click, ctrl-click or marquee exists, so no bulk action on files or tiles is possible. (2) Nothing is discoverable: no cheat sheet, tooltip, help overlay or first-run anywhere in the shell; park, close, restore and reset have no chord and live only in a right-click menu the user must guess is there; the action manifest can already generate a cheat sheet and nothing renders one. (3) No file operations from Home: navigate and open only — no rename, copy, move, new folder, properties or clipboard, and no drag of a file into an application; Operation::OpenWith and AddReference return None (field_screen.rs:1435). (4) The trash could not list its contents. (5) Accessibility is claimed but not built.

DOCUMENTED-BUT-ABSENT, which is a distinct and worse category than merely missing, because the docs assert it: docs/architecture/accessibility.md claims AT-SPI support and a high-contrast variant for every shell surface; no atspi dependency exists in any Cargo.toml and no contrast token or theme exists in shell/lege-shell/src. a11y.seed installs Orca with nothing to read, because the shell paints itself with a custom rasterizer and exposes no accessible name, role or state for any tile, row or widget. Reduced motion and the focus ring are real and respected; the rest of the claim is not implemented.

ABSENT WITH NO SUBSTITUTE: Lifecycle1.Lock hard-fails NotSupported although the compositor fully implements ext-session-lock-v1 — nothing drives it; volume, brightness and battery exist nowhere in the tree as code, not as stubs; the Files app has no new folder, search, sort control, view mode or breadcrumbs, though lege-filed supports CreateDirectory; the OpenURI, Screenshot, ScreenCast and Print portals do not exist; no removable-media mount or eject; no display configuration; no keyboard-layout switcher, touchpad settings or IME.

STALE LEDGER CLAIMS corrected by this audit: the graphical settings app and the shell's notification rendering both shipped on 2026-08-30, after the 08-27 readiness audit that called them stubs, and the portal NoUiAvailable path is now a headless-only fallback rather than the default.

### Hot-fixability and daily-development readiness, 2026-08-31

`verified` · `@legeos.assessment.hotfixability-current-state-20260831/2` · scope `path "crates/lege-state/**"`, `path "debian/**"`, `path "distro/**"`, `path "docs/planning/**"`, `path "installer/**"`, `path "packaging/**"`, `path "scripts/reinstall-legeos-desktop.sh"`, `path "services/lege-hostd/**"`, `path "session/units/**"`

LegeOS is currently suitable for active development as an additional desktop session on a stable Ubuntu host with the host session, display manager, TTY and backups retained as recovery paths. Stage-1 packages can be installed while the old session runs; applications, shell and separated services provide progressively restartable activation boundaries, while the compositor honestly requires logout and kernel/driver/boot changes require a staged reboot. It is not yet suitable as the sole recoverable bare-metal daily driver because installer/ISO and clean-install gates are unfinished, boot-deployment rollback is not hardware-proven and ADR-0004 remains open, coordinated service restart and cross-version state/IPC skew are unproven, and the archive path is inconsistent with the Rust 1.97 workspace and still has sibling path dependencies.

**depends_on** `@legeos.decision.compositor-on-smithay/1`, `@legeos.work.desktop-validation-foundations/1` · **supersedes** `@legeos.assessment.hotfixability-current-state-20260831/1` · **derived_from** `@legeos.assessment.desktop-test-readiness-20260827/1`

### baseline + btrfs delta equals a fresh direct scan, field for field, on the fifth fixture run

`verified` · `@legeos.evidence.btrfs-delta-correctness-gate-passes/1`

Run by the user as root against the loopback Btrfs fixture on 2026-09-04. All five harness tests pass in 352 s. The gate is that an index carried forward only by decoded btrfs send --no-data streams equals an index built from nothing against the final tree, compared field for field on path, kind, size, alloc, mtime, ctime, mode, hidden, dev, inode and nlink; a third arm carried forward by today's reconcile is compared too, as a check on the harness itself. It holds across 24 scenario/tree-size rows (1,540 / 15,339 / 153,327 entries; nothing at all, 100 new files, an hour of desktop use, a 5,000-file build burst, a whole-directory rename, a mass delete, one 1 GiB file, truncate-chmod-rewrite-in-place). The edge-case round trip covering hard links, symlinks, a whole-directory rename, a rename cycle and a move onto an occupied path reports planned_paths 10, mutations 11, creates 3, removes 1, moves 5, touches 2 — exactly what the in-tree test encoder predicted before the fixture confirmed it. An interrupted delta is refused rather than half-applied at all 64 truncated prefixes of a 7,360-byte stream. This was the fifth run: four earlier ones failed, each on a real bug (@legeos.observation.a-send-stream-names-paths-relative-to-the-subvolume-not-the-index-root, @legeos.observation.a-directory-whose-contents-changed-kept-a-stale-modification-time).

### lege doctor --hardware now executes ten bounded read-only probes and emits one four-outcome report; every manual case is not-executed

`verified` · `@legeos.evidence.hardware-qualification-report-20260903/1`

On the Intel Iris Xe + RTX 4060 Laptop dev host: 39 findings — 20 pass, 1 fail, 7 skipped, 11 not executed (report kept at .agent/scratch/de01/D4-doctor-hardware.json via `akr scratch keep`). Ten probes ran read-only and timeout-bounded: kernel-release (6.17.0-41-generic), drm-connected-output (card2-eDP-2), drm-modesetting, nvidia-module (610.43.02 matches nvidia-driver-610-open), nvidia-smi (RTX 4060 Laptop GPU), vulkan-devices (3 devices), prime-offload (available, not exercised), vaapi (59 profiles, Intel iHD 25.4.5) all passed; cuda-device-query was skipped (deviceQuery is not installed). nvidia-module-signer FAILED: the module is signed by a locally enrolled MOK with no linux-modules-nvidia-* package installed — this host is DKMS-built, which LegeOS forbids. All eleven tests/hardware cases were emitted as not-executed with their steps. NOTHING MANUAL RAN: no suspend, reboot, GPU-mode change, cable operation or driver change was performed or attempted, and no hardware case may be read as passed.

### The idle index watcher went from 121 wakeups per minute to none, measured against a binary built from the pre-fix commit

`verified` · `@legeos.evidence.idle-index-wakeups-eliminated-20260904/1` · scope `path "services/lege-filed/src/watcher.rs"`, `path "tools/xtask/src/index_bench.rs"`

Over a 60 second settled idle window with one armed fixture root, the pre-fix binary (built from a git worktree at the parent of commit 6522e10, so this is a true before/after rather than a recollection) recorded 121 timeslices and 120 voluntary context switches; after the fix both are 0. read_bytes, syscw and wchar were already 0 on this workload in both builds, so the gain is wakeups and the roots-table write per tick, not read I/O. Measured from /proc/<tid>/schedstat and /proc/<pid>/status for the lege-index-watcher thread. The harness had to be an xtask subcommand rather than a benches/ target, because watch::guard panics on any real watch root when the executable path contains a deps component, which is true of every cargo bench and integration-test binary; this was verified directly rather than assumed. Four defects in the harness itself were found and fixed during the run: a wrong schedstat field index, per-task versus per-process voluntary_ctxt_switches, a pid-matching bug against a leaked process, and the sandbox-specific discovery that File::set_modified raises no inotify event here while touch(1) does.

**derived_from** `@legeos.work.adaptive-index-maintenance/1`

### M1: a trial boot can fail because the session never came up

`verified` · `@legeos.evidence.m1-boot-health-can-fail/1`

lege-sessiond reports session health to lege-hostd at the moment it signals systemd readiness, so an absent session-healthy marker now means the session did not come up rather than that nobody could report it. The compositor-active marker stays deliberately unwired and reports Skipped, because sessiond has no honest evidence for it; the two switches are separate so arming one never arms the other. A skip never arms a reboot, and only a boot genuinely trialling a candidate can force one.

### M1: the checkpoint protocol is deliverable end to end, and verifies its peer

`verified` · `@legeos.evidence.m1-checkpoint-transport/1`

org.legeos.Checkpoint1 is served by an application instance and called by lege-sessiond on the governor's behalf, addressed by a bus name derived from the InstanceId so nothing is registered and no directory goes stale. The daemon resolves the claimed name's PID and confirms its cgroup names that exact instance before believing any answer — an application squatting another instance's name is refused without being called — and every call is bounded by the request's own deadline, so a peer barely responsive under the pressure that prompted the request is refused rather than hanging the relay.

### The fixture half of rollback acceptance: pruning never drops the set a rollback would need, rolling back is the same path with the previous set, an apt success that did not take is a failure, a unit that comes back running the old build is not activated (one retry then stop and offer rollback), and the dry run prints the publish, pinned apt line, gate verdicts and per-component plan against a scratch build set. The live half — break lege-shell deliberately, confirm the health gate refuses before logout, lege dev rollback restores without rebuilding — is a hands-on user step still pending.
